title: Flush toilet
description: Carries waste away and keeps the smell out of the house. Pulling a handle opens a valve so water from a cistern rushes through the bowl and down the drain. Afterwards some water stays trapped in a bend of the pipe, a plug of liquid that sewer gas cannot get past.
draw: Cutaway side view of a toilet with a cistern above it and the drain pipe beneath curving down, up and over in an S shape; the water standing in the bowl and in the lowest bend of the S is one continuous pool, level on both sides, and a lever on the cistern lifts a valve in its base.
flag: Sir John Harington built a flushing water closet in 1596; Cumming's 1775 patent added the S-bend trap. Cumming was Scottish but worked in London.

title: Dishwasher
description: Washes a load of plates without anyone scrubbing them. Dishes stand in wire racks while a pump sprays very hot, soapy water up at them from arms below; the jets push the arms round so the spray sweeps every plate. Cochrane's first machine turned a wheel of racks through jets of hot water instead.
draw: Cutaway front view of a dishwasher with its door open: plates standing upright in a wire rack, and below them a flat spray arm on a central pivot with angled nozzles, jets of water fanning upward onto the plates; the arm spins horizontally, parallel to the floor.
flag: 1886 is Cochrane's patent; her machines sold mainly to hotels and restaurants after the 1893 Chicago fair. Electric home dishwashers came in the 1920s to 1950s.

title: Vacuum cleaner
description: Sucks dust out of carpets instead of just stirring it into the air. A motor spins a fan that throws air out of the machine, lowering the pressure inside, so outside air rushes in through the nozzle, dragging dirt with it. A cloth bag or filter lets the air out but keeps the dust.
draw: Cutaway of an upright vacuum cleaner on a carpet: an electric motor turning a fan in a housing just above the floor nozzle, the fan blowing air up into a tall cloth bag on the handle; arrows show air going from the carpet into the nozzle, and dust is caught inside the bag.
flag: Booth's 1901 machine was a horse-drawn, petrol-engined pump parked outside the house with hoses fed through the windows; the portable electric upright came from James Spangler in 1907 (sold by Hoover from 1908).

title: Water chlorination
description: Makes tap water safe from cholera and typhoid. A small, measured dose of chlorine is mixed into the water at the treatment works, where it chemically burns through the outer walls and enzymes of bacteria and kills them. A faint trace stays in the pipes, so germs that get in later die too.
draw: A water treatment works: a dosing pipe from a tank of chlorine solution dripping steadily into the channel where water flows into a large open concrete basin of clear water, with a pipe leading on from the basin toward a distant town.
flag: Input said 1908 (Jersey City, John Leal: first continuous use in the US). First permanent chlorination was Lincoln, England, 1905 (Houston and McGowan); Middelkerke, Belgium chlorinated continuously from 1902. Chose 1905.

title: Zipper
description: Closes a jacket, bag or tent in one pull. Each metal or plastic tooth has a bump on top and a hollow underneath; the Y-shaped slider bends the two rows apart and feeds them together at an angle, so each tooth nests between two teeth on the other side and the bumps lock into the hollows.
draw: Close-up of a metal zip half done up on a jacket, closed end at the bottom: below the slider the two rows of teeth are meshed in a single tight line; above it they spread apart in a V. The slider is a small Y-shaped channel with a wedge inside its wide top end that pushes the rows apart, and a pull tab hanging from its front.
flag: Whitcomb Judson's 'clasp locker' (1893) came first but jammed; Sundback's 1913 'Hookless No. 2' is the modern design.

title: Sewage treatment
description: Cleans a town's waste water before it goes back into a river. Sewage is held in tanks while air is bubbled through it, and swarms of bacteria eat the dissolved filth; the bacteria clump into a sludge that settles out, leaving clear water, and some of the sludge is fed back to start on the next batch.
draw: A long rectangular open concrete tank of brown water seen from slightly above, with air bubbles boiling up evenly across the whole surface from pipes along the bottom; beside it a round settling tank with a slowly rotating bridge arm and clear water spilling over its rim.
flag: Card describes the activated-sludge process (Ardern and Lockett, Manchester, 1914). Simpler sewage treatment (sewage farms, trickling filters) is older; 'Activated sludge' would be a more exact title.

title: Frozen food
description: Keeps food tasting fresh for months. Packed food is pressed between metal plates or belts chilled far below freezing, so it freezes solid in minutes rather than hours. Fast freezing forms ice crystals too small to burst the food's cells, so it is not mushy when thawed.
draw: Two long stainless-steel conveyor belts running one above the other, sandwiching a row of flat cardboard cartons of food between them; the belts are thick with frost, and icy brine sprays onto their outer faces from pipes above and below. At the far end the cartons come out frozen hard.
flag: 1924 is when Birdseye founded General Seafood to quick-freeze fish; frozen food first went on sale in shops in 1930 (Springfield, Massachusetts).

title: Polyethylene
description: The commonest plastic, used for bags, bottles, film and cable insulation. It is made by linking thousands of small molecules of ethylene gas end to end into long chains of carbon atoms; the tangled chains slide past each other when warm, so it can be moulded, but hold together as a tough, waxy solid when cool.
draw: A crinkled, translucent milky-white plastic carrier bag lying open beside a small heap of the white plastic pellets it is made from.
flag: Title changed from 'Plastics (polyethylene)': plastics as such predate it (Bakelite, 1907). 1933 is the accidental discovery at ICI Northwich; production began 1939. The hint's 'isotactic polymers' belongs to the later Ziegler-Natta catalysts (1953).

title: Gas-turbine power station
description: Makes electricity from natural gas with what is essentially a jet engine bolted to the ground. A compressor squeezes air, gas burns in it, and the hot blast spins a turbine that drives a generator. Most modern plants then use the exhaust to boil water for a second, steam turbine, turning about 60 percent of the fuel's energy into electricity.
draw: Cutaway of a long horizontal gas turbine in a power hall: rows of compressor blades narrowing from the air inlet, a ring of flames in the middle, larger turbine blades after it, all on one shaft that continues into a large generator, with a duct from the hot exhaust end leading to a boiler.
flag: Re 'are these common?': yes, gas plants make about a fifth of the world's electricity and around 40% in the US, mostly combined-cycle. First gas-turbine power station: Neuchatel, Switzerland, 1939 (Brown Boveri); combined cycle from about 1960 (Korneuburg, Austria), widespread from the 1990s (the input year 1990). Chose 1939.

title: Randomized controlled trial
inventor: Austin Bradford Hill, Medical Research Council
description: A fair test of whether a treatment works. Patients are split into two groups purely by chance, for instance by sealed envelopes, and one group gets the treatment while the other does not. Chance spreads age, health and every hidden difference evenly, so any gap in how the groups fare is down to the treatment.
draw: On a hospital bedside table, a doctor's hand draws a card out of one of a stack of identical sealed envelopes; beside it stand two identical medicine bottles, one with a white cap and one with a blue cap, standing for the two groups. A hospital bed is softly visible behind.
flag: 1948 is the MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis. James Lind's 1747 scurvy test was controlled but not randomized.

title: Credit card
inventor: Frank McNamara and Ralph Schneider, Diners Club
description: Lets you buy now and pay later without carrying cash. The card names your account; the shop passes the charge to the card company, which pays the shop and sends you one bill a month. Later cards held the account number in a magnetic stripe, as tiny magnetised patches a reader senses, and now in a chip.
draw: A hand swiping a plain plastic card through the slot of a countertop card reader, the dark magnetic stripe on the back of the card facing into the slot where the reading head sits. No lettering or logos on the card or the reader.
flag: Diners Club (1950) was a cardboard charge card paid off monthly; BankAmericard (1958) was the first widely used revolving-credit card, and the magnetic stripe came from IBM in the 1960s.

title: Centre-pivot irrigation
description: Waters a whole field with almost no labour. A long pipe carried on wheeled steel towers turns slowly round a well at the centre like the hand of a clock, spraying water from sprinklers along its length; each tower is driven forward by its own motor, so the arm sweeps out a giant green circle.
draw: A centre-pivot irrigator in a crop field seen from a low angle: a long horizontal water pipe held up by tall A-frame towers on pairs of large rubber-tyred wheels, braced by trusses underneath, with sprinklers hanging down spraying water, and the fixed central pivot tower at the far end.
flag: Zybach built a prototype around 1948 near Strasburg, Colorado; patent and first full five-tower system 1952. Early machines were driven by water pressure; electric drives came later.

title: Nuclear submarine
description: A submarine that can stay underwater for months, not hours. In its reactor, splitting uranium heats water in a sealed loop; that water boils water in a second loop into steam, which spins a turbine to drive the propeller. Because nothing burns, it needs no air, and its time submerged is limited mainly by the crew's food.
draw: Cutaway side view of a long, rounded submarine underwater: a reactor in a thick shielded compartment amidships, steam pipes running aft to a turbine, and a single shaft from the turbine to one propeller at the stern. The sail (conning tower) rises from the top of the hull ahead of the reactor.
flag: USS Nautilus was commissioned in September 1954 but first got under way on nuclear power in January 1955. Overlaps Submarine (1898) and Controlled fission reactors (1954).

title: Disposable syringe
description: Gives injections with a needle used once and thrown away, so it cannot carry disease from one patient to the next. A rubber-tipped plunger seals against the wall of a clear plastic barrel: pulling it back lowers the pressure inside, and the outside air pressure pushes medicine up through the hollow steel needle.
draw: A clear plastic syringe with fine graduation lines (no numbers), its rubber-tipped plunger pulled halfway back, held upright beneath an upside-down glass vial; the steel needle pierces the vial's rubber stopper and liquid is rising into the barrel.
flag: First is disputed: Roehr Products (US) sold a plastic disposable syringe in 1955, Charles Rothauser (Australia) reportedly made one in 1949, Murdoch patented his in 1956, and Becton Dickinson's Plastipak (1961) made them common.

title: Flexible endoscope
inventor: Basil Hirschowitz, Larry Curtiss, Wilbur Peters
description: Lets a doctor look inside the stomach without surgery. A bendable tube holds a bundle of thousands of glass fibres, each thinner than a hair and kept in the same order at both ends; light bounces along inside each fibre without escaping, so together they carry a picture round corners, while other fibres carry light in.
draw: A long black flexible tube curving in a loop, its tip glowing with light, with the tip cut away to show a dense bundle of hair-thin glass fibres inside; at the other end a control handle with an eyepiece for the doctor.
flag: University of Michigan; first used on a patient in 1957. Today's endoscopes mostly use a tiny camera chip at the tip instead of a fibre image bundle.

title: Three-point seat belt
description: Holds you in your seat in a crash instead of letting you fly into the windscreen. One belt runs low across the hips and diagonally across the chest, anchored at three points, so the force lands on the strong pelvis and ribcage. A weighted catch in the reel locks the belt when the car brakes hard.
draw: A driver sitting in a car seat wearing a three-point belt: the lap part lies low across the hips, and the shoulder part runs diagonally from a mount on the door pillar above the outer shoulder, across the chest, down to a buckle beside the inner hip. The belt comes out of a reel low on the door pillar.
flag: The first 1959 Volvo belts were fixed; inertia-locking reels came a few years later.

title: Planetary space probe
description: A robot spacecraft sent to fly past or orbit another planet and report back. Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, small thrusters keep it pointed the right way, and instruments measure what it passes. A dish antenna aimed at Earth sends the readings home as a faint radio signal that giant dishes pick up.
draw: A spacecraft in space with a central boxy body, two flat rectangular solar panels spread out like wings, and a dish antenna on an arm pointed back toward a small blue Earth, while a large, cloud-covered pale yellow planet fills the other side of the frame.
flag: Mariner 2 flew past Venus on 14 December 1962, the first probe to work at another planet (Soviet Venera 1, 1961, went silent on the way). Title made singular to match the deck.

title: Carbon-fibre composites
inventor: William Watt, Leslie Phillips, William Johnson, Royal Aircraft Establishment
description: Makes parts stiffer and stronger than steel for their weight, for aircraft, racing bikes and tennis rackets. Threads of nearly pure carbon, each finer than a hair, are laid in the directions the load will pull and set in a hard, glue-like resin; the fibres carry the force and the resin holds them in shape.
draw: Close-up of a sheet of carbon-fibre composite with a broken edge: a glossy black resin surface showing the woven checkerboard of fibre bundles, and at the snapped edge individual hair-fine black fibres sticking out of the resin.
flag: RAE Farnborough process, 1963. Roger Bacon (Union Carbide, 1958) and Akio Shindo (Japan, 1961) made earlier strong carbon fibres.

title: Drip irrigation
description: Waters crops a drop at a time right at the roots, using far less water than flooding or sprinklers. Plastic tubes run along each row with small drippers set into them. Inside each dripper the water squeezes through a long, narrow zigzag channel whose friction soaks up the pressure, so it seeps out slowly and evenly all along the line.
draw: Ground-level close-up of a black plastic tube lying along a row of young plants in dry soil; a small dripper in the tube releases a single drop beside one plant's stem, where a dark circle of damp soil has spread.
flag: Blass's agreement with Kibbutz Hatzerim, which founded Netafim, was signed in 1965; the first commercial drippers were sold in 1966.

title: Fax machine
description: Sends a copy of a page across the world over an ordinary phone line. The sending machine scans the page line by line, a light-sensitive cell turning each spot's lightness or darkness into an electrical tone; the receiving machine listens to the tones and prints matching dots, line by line, to rebuild the page.
draw: A desktop fax machine with a telephone handset resting on top, a sheet of paper being drawn face-down into its slot over a narrow bright strip of scanning light that shines across the full width of the page.
flag: Year changed from 1964 to 1966: Xerox's 1964 LDX needed special lines, while the 1966 Magnafax Telecopier (built with Magnavox) was the first to work over ordinary phone lines. Facsimile is far older: Caselli's pantelegraph ran a service in France in the 1860s, and newspapers sent wirephotos from the 1920s.

title: Oral rehydration therapy
description: Saves people dying of diarrhoea with a drink of clean water, salt and sugar. Cholera makes the gut pour out water faster than a body can safely lose it. But the gut lining has carriers that pull salt and sugar in together, and water follows them by osmosis, so the drink is soaked up even while the diarrhoea goes on.
draw: A mother holding a cup to a small child's lips; on the table beside them are a jug of water, a little heap of salt, a heap of sugar and a spoon.
flag: First clinical trial at the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka (then East Pakistan) in 1968; Norbert Hirschhorn (1968) and Dilip Mahalanabis (refugee camps, 1971) are also credited.

title: Email
description: Sends a written message to someone's computer mailbox in seconds. The message is addressed with a person's name, an @ sign and the name of their computer, and is passed from machine to machine over the network until it reaches that one. There it waits in the person's mailbox file until they log in to read it.
draw: A 1970s computer terminal: a typewriter-style keyboard with a roll of paper rising above it, a printed message shown as rows of indistinct grey lines on the paper, and a thick cable running from it to a tall cabinet of computer equipment.
flag: Tomlinson's 1971 mail between two ARPANET computers is the usual credit; messages between users of one shared computer (MIT's CTSS) date from 1965.

title: Graphical user interface
description: Lets people use a computer by pointing at pictures instead of typing commands. Every dot on the screen is a bit in the computer's memory, so it can draw overlapping windows, icons and menus; a hand-held mouse moves an arrow across them, and clicking a picture carries out its command.
draw: A desktop computer with an upright, portrait-shaped screen showing overlapping rectangular windows, small icons and an arrow pointer (no readable text), with a keyboard in front and a three-button mouse on the desk beside it, its cable running to the computer.
flag: 1973 is the Xerox Alto, used inside Xerox. Douglas Engelbart showed windows and a mouse in 1968; the Apple Macintosh (1984) brought the idea to the public.

title: Pulse oximeter
description: Clips on a fingertip and shows how much oxygen the blood is carrying. Two tiny lights, one red and one infrared, shine through the finger to a light sensor on the other side. Oxygen-rich blood lets more red light through than oxygen-poor blood does, so comparing the two colours as each heartbeat swells the arteries gives the reading.
draw: Cutaway of a clip-on sensor gripping a fingertip: two tiny lights in the upper jaw (one glowing red, one infrared shown as a faint dark-red glow) shine down through the finger, past its small arteries, onto a light sensor in the lower jaw.
flag: Input said 1974. Aoyagi worked out the principle in 1972 and presented it in 1974; Nihon Kohden's first (ear) oximeter went on sale in 1975. Fingertip clips became common in the 1980s.

title: Waterproof breathable fabric
inventor: Bob Gore, W. L. Gore & Associates
description: Keeps rain out while letting sweat escape, so a jacket stays dry inside. A thin film of stretched non-stick plastic (PTFE) is bonded inside the cloth; it is full of billions of tiny pores, far too small for a raindrop to squeeze through but much bigger than single molecules of water vapour, which drift out.
draw: Magnified cross-section of a jacket fabric: an outer woven layer with round raindrops beaded on top, a thin white membrane beneath riddled with tiny pores, and wisps of water vapour rising up through the pores from the warm body side below, while the drops stay on top.
flag: Changed from 1969: Bob Gore stretched PTFE into a porous membrane in 1969, but the first Gore-Tex fabric went on sale in 1976. Tightly woven Ventile cotton (England, 1940s) was an earlier waterproof breathable cloth.

title: Anti-lock brakes
description: Stops a car's wheels locking and skidding in hard braking, so the car can still be steered. A toothed ring and a magnetic sensor at each wheel report how fast it turns. If one wheel slows much faster than the car, a microchip has valves release and reapply its brake many times a second, keeping the tyre just short of skidding.
draw: Close-up behind a car wheel: a brake disc gripped by its caliper, and beside the hub a toothed metal ring turning with the wheel, with a small sensor tip mounted just clear of the teeth and a wire leading away from it.
flag: 1978 is Bosch's digital system on the Mercedes S-Class, the usual 'first'; Chrysler and Bendix sold electronic four-wheel anti-lock on the 1971 Imperial, and Dunlop's mechanical Maxaret was used on aircraft from the 1950s and on the Jensen FF car in 1966.

title: Hepatitis B vaccine
inventor: Baruch Blumberg, Irving Millman; Maurice Hilleman, Merck
description: Protects against a virus that causes liver failure and liver cancer; it was the first vaccine to prevent a cancer. It contains harmless copies of the virus's outer protein, which train the immune system to recognise the real thing; since 1986 that protein has been made by yeast cells given the virus gene, instead of purified from infected blood.
draw: A nurse's gloved hand giving a baby a vaccine injection in the thigh, with a small glass vial of cloudy white vaccine and a syringe on a tray beside them.
flag: 1981 is the US licence of the first vaccine, purified from carriers' blood plasma. The recombinant, yeast-made version the hint describes was licensed in 1986.

title: Mobile phone
description: A telephone you carry, so you can call from almost anywhere. The land is divided into small cells, each with its own radio mast; the phone talks to the nearest one and is handed on to the next as you move. Cells far enough apart reuse the same frequencies, so millions of people can call at once.
draw: A hand holding a large brick-shaped handheld phone with a keypad and a stubby rubber antenna on top, raised toward the ear; behind, out of focus, a lattice-steel radio mast with flat panel antennas near its top.
flag: Cooper made the first handheld call in 1973; the DynaTAC went on sale with the first US cell network in 1983. Japan (1979) and Scandinavia (1981) had cellular car-phone networks first.

title: Internet
description: Links the world's computer networks into one. Every message is chopped into small packets, each labelled with where it is going; routers along the way pass each packet on toward its destination by whatever path is free, and the receiving computer puts them back in order and asks again for any that went missing.
draw: A single network router box with blinking lights and many cables plugged into its back, the cables fanning out to a laptop, a desktop computer and a fibre-optic cable whose cut end glows with light.
flag: 1 January 1983: ARPANET switched to Cerf and Kahn's TCP/IP, the usual birth date. Overlaps with the World Wide Web card.

title: Flash memory
description: Keeps photos, music and files when the power is off, in phones, cameras and memory sticks. Each bit is a little charge of electrons trapped on an island of conductor sealed in very thin insulation above a transistor. A high voltage pushes electrons through the insulation by quantum tunnelling, and the trapped charge decides whether the transistor switches on.
draw: A memory stick with its plastic casing opened: a small green circuit board carrying a flat black memory chip, a smaller controller chip, and a metal plug connector at one end.
flag: Masuoka invented flash at Toshiba (NOR type shown 1984, NAND 1987); Intel sold the first flash chips in 1988, and Toshiba's NAND reached the market about 1989.

title: Rapid test strip
inventor: Unipath, Unilever (Keith May, Mick Prior, Ian Richards)
description: Gives a yes-or-no medical answer in minutes at home, as in pregnancy and Covid tests. A drop of urine or swab fluid soaks along a paper strip, picking up antibodies stuck to tiny coloured particles; if the substance being tested for is there, it links those particles to a line of other antibodies fixed across the strip, and a coloured line appears.
draw: A plastic test cassette lying flat, cut away to show the paper strip inside: a pad at one end with a drop of liquid soaking in, the wet front creeping along the strip, and two coloured lines showing in the result window.
flag: Clearblue One Step pregnancy test, Unipath (Unilever), Bedford, 1988: the first lateral-flow test on sale.

title: World Wide Web
description: Turns the internet into a library anyone can browse. Pages are stored on computers called servers, each page with its own address; a browser program asks for a page, gets back text marked up with formatting and links, and clicking a link fetches another page from wherever in the world it lives.
draw: A boxy 1990s desktop computer whose screen shows a page of pictures and blocks of grey lines standing for text, a few highlighted links among them, with a hand on the mouse about to click one.
flag: Proposed 1989, first website December 1990, opened to the public August 1991. CERN straddles the Swiss-French border.

title: Online shopping
description: Lets people buy almost anything from home and have it delivered. A shop's website lists its goods; the customer's card number is scrambled by encryption on its way to the shop's computer, which checks it with the bank, and a warehouse then picks, packs and posts the order.
draw: A cardboard parcel just delivered on a doorstep, beside it through the open door a laptop on a hall table whose screen shows a grid of product pictures with one highlighted, and a bank card resting by the keyboard.
flag: Changed from 1995: the first secure web purchase was NetMarket's sale of a CD in August 1994 (Dan Kohn, Philadelphia). Amazon and eBay opened in 1995; Michael Aldrich's teleshopping over a phone line and TV (England, 1979) is an earlier claim. Inventor left blank as collective.

title: White LED lighting
description: Lights homes and streets on a fraction of a bulb's electricity and lasts for decades. A tiny chip of gallium nitride glows blue when current flows through it; a coating of yellow phosphor over the chip turns some of that blue light into yellow, and the blue and yellow together look white.
draw: Close-up cutaway of a single white LED: a tiny square chip glowing blue in a small metal cup, a blob of yellow phosphor covering it, and white light spreading out of the top, with two wire legs leading out below.
flag: Nichia's blue-chip-plus-yellow-phosphor white LED, 1996. Overlaps with any blue LED card (Nakamura, 1993).

title: Wireless network
description: Connects laptops, phones and printers to the internet without cables, across a home or office. A router and each device trade short radio bursts at a few billion waves a second. Newer versions split the data across dozens of neighbouring frequencies sent at once, which the receiving chip separates by Fourier analysis, so echoes off walls do not scramble it.
draw: A home wireless router on a wooden shelf: a flat box with three upright antennas and a row of small indicator lights, a laptop open on a table nearby, with faint concentric ripples spreading from the antennas to suggest radio waves.
flag: Title changed from 'Wi-Fi', a trademark. 1997 is the first standard (IEEE 802.11, committee chaired by Vic Hayes of NCR); NCR's WaveLAN (Netherlands, 1991) came before, and home use spread from 1999. The many-frequency method (OFDM) came with 802.11a/g (1999-2003), using a CSIRO (Australia) patent.

title: Ion thruster
description: Pushes a spacecraft for months on end using a tenth of a rocket's fuel. Powered by solar panels, it strips electrons off xenon atoms, and charged metal grids at the back fling the ions out at about 30 kilometres a second. The push is as gentle as a sheet of paper resting on your hand, but never lets up.
draw: The back of a spacecraft with large solar panels: a round thruster whose face is a slightly domed metal grid pierced with thousands of tiny holes, from which a faint glowing blue plume streams straight back into black space.
flag: Re Boris's note: thrust is tiny (Deep Space 1's was under a tenth of a newton) but it uses about ten times less propellant than a chemical rocket, so it wins on long missions. 1998 is Deep Space 1, the first probe driven mainly by one; Kaufman's design first flew on SERT 1 (1964). Ion and related Hall thrusters now drive probes like Dawn and keep thousands of communications satellites in orbit.

title: Continuous glucose monitor
description: Tracks blood sugar day and night for people with diabetes, without finger-prick tests. A hair-thin wire under the skin is coated with an enzyme that reacts with sugar in the body's fluid, making a tiny electric current: more sugar, more current. A small transmitter turns that into a reading every few minutes and can pass it to an insulin pump.
draw: Cutaway of the skin of a person's upper arm: a small round disc stuck on the surface, with a single hair-thin flexible wire running from it down into the fatty layer just below the skin, surrounded by cells bathed in fluid.
flag: Title narrowed: monitor and insulin pump are two devices. MiniMed's first monitor (US approval June 1999) recorded for three days for a doctor to read; real-time home monitors came 2004-06. Wearable insulin pumps date from Dean Kamen's of 1976, linked pump-and-sensor systems from 2006. Could be two cards.

title: Video calling
description: Lets people talk face to face across the world, seeing each other as they speak. A small camera captures about thirty pictures a second; software squeezes them by sending mostly what changed since the last picture, breaks them into packets and sends them over the internet, where the other computer rebuilds and shows them alongside the sound.
draw: A laptop open on a kitchen table, a small camera lens in the frame above its screen; on the screen a grandmother's face, smiling and waving, while a child sitting in front of the laptop waves back.
flag: Collective. 2003 is when free internet video calls reached ordinary users (Apple's iChat AV with a webcam; Skype launched that year but added video in 2006). AT&T's Picturephone offered video calls over phone lines in 1964-70.

title: Smartphone
description: A pocket computer that is also a telephone, camera, map and music player. A glass touchscreen senses fingers by the electric charge they draw, and inside are radios for calls, data and satellite positioning, a camera chip and a lithium-ion battery. A microscopic weight on springs inside a chip senses tilt, so the screen turns to match the phone.
draw: A plain smartphone with no logos or buttons held sideways in a hand, partly cut away to show its thin layers: the glass screen on top, a flat battery filling most of the body, and a small circuit board with chips near one end beside a camera lens.
flag: IBM's Simon (1994) is usually called the first smartphone; 2007 marks the touchscreen type with motion sensor, GPS and camera that the hint describes.

title: Quadcopter drone
description: A small flying camera that anyone can steer. Four propellers on electric motors lift it, two spinning clockwise and two anticlockwise so the craft doesn't twirl; a computer reads tiny gyroscopes hundreds of times a second and speeds up or slows each motor to keep it level, tilt it and steer.
draw: A small quadcopter hovering, seen from slightly above: an X-shaped frame with a motor and two-bladed propeller at the tip of each of its four arms, diagonally opposite propellers turning the same way and neighbouring ones the opposite way, and a camera hanging below the central body.
flag: Parrot AR.Drone, shown January 2010, the first mass-market quadcopter. Earlier hobby quadcopters existed (Draganflyer, Canada, late 1990s); DJI's Phantom (2013) made camera drones common.

title: Deep learning
inventor: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton
description: Lets computers recognise faces, speech and objects in photos by learning from examples rather than rules. Each example passes through many stacked layers of simple number-crunching units; whenever the answer comes out wrong, every connection is nudged slightly in the direction that would have shrunk the error, millions of times over.
draw: A photo of a cat on the left feeding into a column of glowing dots, then several more columns of dots joined by a dense mesh of fine lines, narrowing to a single bright dot on the right; the lines carrying strong signals glow brighter.
flag: AlexNet, University of Toronto, 2012, won the ImageNet image contest by a wide margin. Deep networks for speech recognition worked a year or two earlier; the training method (backpropagation) dates from the 1980s.

title: mRNA vaccines
inventor: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman; BioNTech, Moderna
description: Teaches the immune system to recognise a virus without meeting it. The injection carries genetic instructions for one virus protein, wrapped in tiny bubbles of fat; muscle cells read the instructions and make the protein, which the immune system learns to attack. The instructions fall apart within days, and the vaccine can be redesigned for a new virus in weeks.
draw: A molecular-scale view at the edge of a cell: a tiny sphere made of fat molecules, partly merged with the cell's outer membrane, releasing coiled single strands of mRNA inside; nearby a ribosome threads along one strand, and spike-shaped proteins stand out on the cell's surface.
flag: Karikó and Weissman (University of Pennsylvania, US) found the key chemical tweak in 2005 (Nobel 2023); the first approved vaccine was Pfizer-BioNTech's (BioNTech is German) in December 2020, with Moderna's (US) days later. Location could be Germany.
